title: The site plan
overview:
Every site has one plan, and it is the single shared picture of the project. It outlives every conversation about the site, so read it before acting on what you think you remember.

The plan has structured parts and a written part. The structured parts are the stages of the build, each not started, in progress or done; the brief, which is the client's goals in structured form; the features they want; the decisions that make up the site, each with a state; the checks — questions put to the consultant and the client — with the answers given; and the tasks. The written part holds the client's goals in their own words, the decision log, and notes.

**A decision has a state, and not objecting is not choosing.** `open` means nobody has decided. `defaulted` means it was picked to get the page built and the client has not really looked. `proposed` means a specific option was put to the client. `not_objected` means the client saw it and said nothing. `chosen`, `delegated` ("you decide") and `parked` ("not now", with a reason) come only from the client, and only with the client's own words attached. Concept-level decisions should end up chosen or delegated; the dangerous gaps are the ones that stayed defaulted.

**Nobody but the consultant and the client answers a check.** The coordinator asks and records; it never has an opinion of the site.

**A change answers what it changed, not the plan.** Every write confirms the one thing it wrote — the decision, task or check as it now stands — with long text shortened. Read the plan when you need the rest of it.

**Asks are the questions waiting for the client.** They show on a panel above the chat, where the client answers them whenever they like, without interrupting the conversation. Put a question there only if the client can answer it unaided and the answer stays true: their phone number, opening hours, the towns they cover, whether they have a price list. Questions of judgement — style, which version they prefer, what to lead with — belong in the conversation. The client owns the answer; you own the wording. Their answers reach you at the start of your next turn.

**Milestones fall due.** When the host sees a moment of the build happen — the first pass built, a round of revisions finished, Publish opened — the checks that moment triggers fall due, and your per-turn plan entry says so. Raise each one with the client in the conversation, and record that you asked (`ask_check`) and what they said (`record_check_answer`). When the entry says the stages are behind the build, catch them up with `set_stage`.

**The stages are the client's progress bar.** The client sees them at the top of the panel: Getting to know you, Looking at other sites, First draft, Refining, Colours & fonts, Finishing touches, Ready to publish. Start a stage (`in_progress`) when the work on it begins, and tick it (`done`) when the client agrees it is done. Only one stage is in progress at a time; starting one moves the marker, and moving forward ticks the stage you leave. They can be done in any order, skipped, or reopened — but a stage passed over shows to the client as skipped, so tick it if it was covered.

**The story board is the client's story in their own words.** It is a third view of the preview, beside View and Edit, and the client sees it before there is any draft. Pin the key things the client says about their business as sticky notes (`pin_notes`) during Getting to know you, and keep pinning as they talk. You may reword a quote so it reads as a note — change person or tense, drop words it does not need — but never add a claim, a fact or an adjective; every note keeps the sentence it came from, which the client sees on hover. Give each note one emoji saying what it is about, and group the notes into themes, at most six, each with its own colour. The client reacts to each note: ❤️ "that's us", 👍 true, 👎 not right or not how they would say it (it stays, pale, and you ask about it or offer a better wording with `reword_note`), or 🗑 delete. They can add notes and edit any note; a note they wrote, edited, hearted or thumbed up is their wording, and you never reword or remove it. When the board has hearts, offer two or three headlines written from the hearted notes (`offer_headlines`) — one line answering why the right customer would pick them over what they would otherwise choose. A new offer never replaces their choice. Their reactions, notes and headline reach you at the start of your next turn. The board never changes the site: the copy is written from the hearted notes and the chosen headline.

plan.plan: the plan's structured parts as they now stand: stages, brief, functionality, decisions, checks, tasks, asks, and the comp board
plan.body: the written part: the client's own words, the decision log, and notes
plan.panel: the same plan projected for a reader: the stages with their words, decisions grouped by state, checks still waiting for an answer, checks that have fallen due and not yet been raised, task progress, and the asks still open
plan.comps: the comp board with each site's likes and dislikes, when it has any sites

written.decision: the decision as it now stands, when the change was to a decision
written.task: the task as it now stands, when the change was to a task
written.check: the check as it now stands, when the change was to a check
written.brief: which parts of the brief were set, when the change was to the brief; `quoted` is true when the client's words were added
written.feature: the feature and its status, when the change was to a feature
written.note: the section and length of the note added, when the change was a note
written.stage: the stage and its state, when the change was to a stage; `moved_from` names the stage that stopped being in progress
written.ask: the ask as it now stands, when the change was to an ask
written.comp: the comp as it now stands, when the change was to the comp board
written.removed: the reference taken off the comp board, or the note taken off the story board
written.notes: the notes just pinned to the story board: each one's id, text and theme
written.note: the story-board note as it now stands
written.theme: the story-board theme as it now stands, with its colour
written.headline: the story board's headline as it now stands: the chosen line, the options still on offer, and the ones offered and passed over

PLAN_INVALID.message: that change would break one of the plan's rules, so nothing was written and the plan is exactly as it was.

UNKNOWN_DECISION.message: the plan has no decision by that id. Read the plan to see the decisions it holds.

UNKNOWN_CHECK.message: the plan has no check by that id. Read the plan to see the checks it holds.

UNKNOWN_TASK.message: the plan has no task by that id. Read the plan to see the tasks it holds.

CONFLICT.message: the plan moved while you were writing. Read it and make your change again; nothing was lost.

SCHEMA_INVALID.message: the change was not well-formed. Nothing was written, and the plan is exactly as it was.

UNKNOWN_ASK.message: the plan has no ask by that id. Read the plan to see the asks it holds; to add one, give it an id, a prompt, a reason and an input.

ASK_WITHDRAWN.message: that ask was withdrawn, and its reason is in the plan. It is not asked again unless you say it applies again.

ASK_ANSWERED.message: the client has answered that ask. Their answer stands; nothing was written.

UNKNOWN_COMP.message: that is not a site on the comp board, or not a capture this business holds. Capture the address with capture_site, then add the reference it answers.

NO_COMPS.message: this host keeps no comp board, so nothing was written.

UNKNOWN_LOOK.message: that is not a look on offer — list the pages to see the looks a set holds. Nothing was written, and the site and the plan are exactly as they were.

CONTENT_CHANGED.message: the look says something different from the page — its words or pictures changed, not only its styling. Nothing was written, and the site and the plan are exactly as they were.

UNKNOWN_NOTE.message: the story board has no note by that id. Read the plan to see the notes it holds.

UNKNOWN_THEME.message: the story board has no theme by that id or name. Read the plan to see its themes.

CLIENTS_WORDS.message: that note is the client's wording — they wrote it, edited it, or gave it a heart or a thumbs-up — so it is theirs and nothing was written. Suggest a change in the conversation instead.

NO_LOOKS.message: this host cannot put a look on the site from the plan, so nothing was written.

operations.summary: Read the site's plan: where the build is, what is decided, what is not.
operations.description: Answers the plan as it stands and a projection of it: decisions grouped by state, checks still waiting for an answer, and task progress. A site nobody has planned yet answers the starting plan, with every decision open.

operations.summary: Record what the client has told you about their business and goals.
operations.description:
Give only the parts you are recording; the rest of the brief is left as it is. Record what the client says — the diagnosis of what will actually help is the consultant's, and belongs in the decisions and tasks, not here.

Pass the client's own words as `quote` whenever you have them. They are kept verbatim in the plan, and they are what a later reader trusts over any summary.

business.description: What the business is and does.

site_job.description: What the site is for right now — separate from who it is for.

audiences.description: Who the site is for, as a list of `{"who": ..., "priority": 1}` with 1 the most important.

goal.description: `{"kind": "leads" | "conversions" | "awareness" | "traffic" | "credibility" | "other", "measure": ..., "proxy": ...}` — what the site should achieve, and how we would know.

quality_bar.description: The standard the client expects, in their words — "premium", "directionally right for a beta".

existing_site.description: `{"url": ..., "feeling": ...}` — any existing site, and how the client feels about it.

constraints.description: Anything the site must or must not do, one string each.

quote.description: What the client said, word for word. Kept in the plan's own-words section.

operations.summary: Record whether the client wants a feature.
operations.description: One feature per call — a contact form, a booking link, a newsletter signup.

status.description: Whether they want it now, not at all, or later.

operations.summary: Add a note to the plan.
operations.description: Anything that helps build the site and is not a decision, a task or part of the brief.

operations.summary: Propose a value for a decision, or mark one you made to get the page built.
operations.description:
When you make a choice so the page can be built, record it as `defaulted` — it is not settled until the client has looked. When you put a specific option to the client, set `proposed`. Only the client settles a decision; you cannot set it chosen, delegated or parked.

To add a decision the plan does not have, give a new id with a title, an area and a tier.

decision.description: The decision's id, as the plan holds it.

value.description: What you picked or are proposing, in plain words.

state.description: `defaulted` for a choice made to get the page built; `proposed` when it has been put to the client.

compared.description: True once the client has seen alternatives side by side.

log.description: The number of the decision-log entry that explains it, if you recorded one.

title.description: For a new decision only: what it is.

tier.description: For a new decision only: `concept` shapes what the site is; `detail` can be settled quickly.

comps.description: The comps (reference uids on the board) that shaped this decision — for example the conventions recorded in `visual_concept`.

operations.summary: Put the look your client chose onto the real page, and record their choice — only when they have said which one they want.
operations.description:
Your client normally does this themselves, with **Choose this one** under the look in the preview's carousel. Use this when they tell you in the conversation instead — never on your own judgement, because it is their decision.

The page keeps its address, title and search description and takes everything the look changed. The choice is recorded as a settled decision in their words, with the set and the looks not chosen. Every look in the set is set aside, out of the carousel; the page as it was is kept as a look labelled "Before …", and choosing that one puts it back.

A look changes how the page looks, never what it says. If the look's words or pictures differ from the page's, this refuses with `CONTENT_CHANGED` and lists what would change. Then either have the look's content put back to the page's, or tell your client exactly what would change and, if they still want it, call again with `content_changes_seen`.

look.description: The page id of the look they chose — from list_pages, where each look carries its set and label.

client_said.description: What your client said when they chose it, in their words. It is recorded with the decision.

content_changes_seen.description: Only after a CONTENT_CHANGED refusal: true when your client has been told what the look changes in the page's words and pictures and still wants it.

operations.summary: Add a task to the plan, or change one.
operations.description: The tasks are your plan for the build. Name no task (or a new id) with a title to add one; name an existing one to change it. Use `depends_on` where one task genuinely has to wait for another — settle what will be copied into every page before building the pages it is copied into.

task.description: The task's id. Omit to add a new task.

depends_on.description: Ids of tasks that must be done first.

decisions.description: Ids of the decisions this task settles or depends on.

operations.summary: Give your answer to a check — "are we happy with …?".
operations.description: Take a position. If the answer is no, say what you would do about it. "It's your call" is not an answer from the expert: give your view, and leave the decision with the client.

note.description: Why, and what you would do if the answer is not yes.

operations.summary: Record what the client said about a decision.
operations.description: You record the client settling a decision; you never settle one yourself. `chosen`, `delegated` and `parked` need the client's own words in `quote`, and `parked` needs the reason it was parked. A settled decision is written into the decision log in the client's words.

state.description: What the client's answer amounts to.

quote.description: What the client said, word for word.

value.description: What was chosen, when it was a choice.

compared.description: True when they chose from alternatives they could see.

parked_reason.description: Why it waits — and so when it should come back.

operations.summary: Record that a check is being asked, which starts a fresh round of answers.
operations.description: Name a standing check, or give a new question. The previous answers are cleared, because they were about a site that has since changed.

check.description: The check's id. Omit to add a new one.

question.description: For a new check: the question, against the brief — never your own opinion.

triggers.description: For a new check: the moments it should be asked again.

operations.summary: Record an answer to a check, from the consultant or the client.
operations.description: Only the consultant (`alice`) and the client (`user`) answer a check. This records what was said: the client's answer as `user`. The consultant's own view goes through `answer_check`, and the coordinator never answers.

note.description: What they said, in their words.

operations.summary: Record a task's progress.
operations.description: Progress only. Adding, ordering and linking tasks is the consultant's.

operations.summary: Mark a stage of the build not started, in progress or done.
operations.description: The client watches these at the top of the panel. Start a stage when the work on it begins; tick it when the client agrees it is done. Starting one moves the in-progress marker off any other: a stage before it is ticked done, a stage after it goes back to not started, and the result says which (moved_from, marked). Any order is fine, and so is reopening a done stage. A stage left not started before the furthest one shows to the client as skipped.

operations.summary: Put a question on the client's panel, or reword one.
operations.description:
Put it there the moment you think of it, rather than holding it for the right moment or asking it in the conversation: a question on the panel costs the client nothing until they choose to answer it. Short prompt that opens with its subject — "Phone number for the site — …", "Photos of your vans — …", never "Could you tell me …" — because the panel folds each question to its first few words; and a one-line reason, which is what makes them bother. Every time you add questions, say so in one line in the conversation, naming them and asking the client to fill them in; never add one silently. Prefer asking for a document over several typed fields: "upload your business card" beats four boxes for address, phone, email and licence number, so set `accepts_upload` wherever a document could answer it. When you ask for files to use on the site, say so with `upload_role: site`; otherwise what arrives is background you can read but never place.

Only facts the client knows and that stay true go here. If you cannot proceed without the answer, ask it in the conversation instead, as the one question of that message.

Editing an ask changes its wording, input or reason and never the client's answer. An ask that was withdrawn is not asked again unless you pass `reopen`.

ask.description: A short id for the ask, e.g. `callout_fee`. A new id adds an ask; an existing one edits it.

prompt.description: The question, short, in the client's words, and opening with its subject, e.g. "Phone number for the site — …".

why.description: One line, shown to the client: why it matters.

input.description: The shape of the answer. `long_text` is for a few sentences or a list. `upload` asks for a document only.

options.description: For `single_choice` and `multi_choice`: the choices, at least two.

accepts_upload.description: True when a document could answer it instead of a typed value.

upload_role.description: For an ask that takes uploads: what the files are FOR. `site` for things the client wants on the site — photographs of their work, their logo — which you can then place. `reference` for background you read — price lists, flyers, old brochures — which can never be placed. Default `reference`, so set `site` whenever you are asking for something to put on the site.

multiple.description: For an ask that takes uploads: true when the client may pick several files at once. Defaults to true for a `site` ask and false otherwise.

needed_by.description: When the answer is needed. It orders the panel and never hides an ask, so a pre-publish detail can sit there from the start. Default `first_pass`.

blocking.description: True when you cannot go on without it.

reopen.description: Ask a withdrawn ask again, because it applies again.

approves.description: A contact detail — an email address, a personal number, a name — you are asking permission to show on the site, e.g. `office@example.com`. The ask becomes a yes-or-no question whose two answers the host words, and the client answering yes approves that detail. Write the prompt so it names the detail and says it would be public.

operations.summary: Put the question of what the site needs to do on the client's panel, tailored from the catalogue.
operations.description:
Raise it once you know a little about the business — after they have told you about it, before the comps — with one line in the conversation first, e.g. "Before I build anything — a few things the site might need to do. I've ticked the ones I'd expect for a plumber; change anything that's wrong." Then post it here.

The options are the capability catalogue (`read_plan` answers it as `feature_catalogue`) and nothing else: things the site DOES. Leave out those that plainly don't apply, tick the ones you expect — the client can untick them — and reword a label for the business ("Patients can book an appointment"); the id stays the same, so the answer still names the capability. The client can also write something else beneath it.

A capability marked not yet available is still offered, and shown to the client as not yet available. Never promise or build one: if they want it, say plainly that it is not offered yet. Their answer fills the plan's features by capability id.

capabilities.description: The catalogue ids to offer, in the order to show them. Omit to offer every one.

ticked.description: Ids, among those offered, to tick in advance because you expect them.

labels.description: A rewording for the business, by id, e.g. {"booking": "Patients can book an appointment"}. Ids you leave out keep the catalogue's words.

prompt.description: The question, if the catalogue's wording does not suit.

why.description: One line on why it matters, if the catalogue's does not suit.

operations.summary: Take a question off the client's panel because it no longer applies.
operations.description: For example, the client says they do not want an email address on the site: withdraw the email ask. It leaves the panel and stays in the plan with your reason, so nobody asks it again. An ask the client has answered cannot be withdrawn.

operations.summary: Record that the client said a contact detail may appear on the site.
operations.description: An email address, a personal phone number, a home address or a person's name goes on a page only once the client has said yes to that detail appearing publicly — a letterhead or an uploaded document is not a yes. When they say yes in the conversation, record it here with their own words; an approval ask they answer yes does the same from the panel. A site change that would show an email address nobody approved is refused until one of the two is recorded.

detail.description: The detail exactly as it will appear, e.g. `office@example.com`.

quote.description: What the client said, word for word.

operations.summary: Answer a question on the panel from something the client uploaded.
operations.description: When a document answers an ask — a business card gives the phone number and address — take the fact from it and fill the ask in, citing the material, so the client sees the question go away. They can still change it. An answer the client gave themselves is never replaced.

material.description: The uid of the material the answer came from.

answer.description: The fact, as taken from the material. For a multi-choice ask, its options separated by `;`. Omit when the document itself is the answer.

operations.summary: Put the comp board — "Sites we're comparing" — on the client's panel.
operations.description: The board is a question like any other: it is not on the client's panel until you raise it. Raise it when you are ready to look at other sites together — after the features question, before the first build — with one line in the conversation first, e.g. "Next, let's look at a few sites in your trade — add any you like, or don't, and I'll find some too." Putting a site on it with `add_comp` raises it as well. Raising it again changes nothing.

operations.summary: Put a captured site on the client's comp board — "Sites we're comparing".
operations.description: Comps are real sites in the client's trade and area that you and the client look at before the first build. Capture the address with `capture_site` first, then give the `reference.uid` it answered. The client sees the site on their plan panel with a thumbnail of its hero, and can open it in the preview pane. Adding a site that is already on the board changes nothing.

reference.description: The reference uid `capture_site` answered for the site.

operations.summary: Record what the client likes and dislikes about a comp, in their words.
operations.description: Short notes, one item each, as the client said them ("phone number in three places", "too many coupons"). Each list you give replaces that list; leave one out to keep it. The client can edit the same notes on their panel, and you are told on your next turn when they do.

likes.description: What the client likes about it, one short item each.

dislikes.description: What the client dislikes about it, one short item each.

operations.summary: Take a site off the comp board.
operations.description: The capture stays in the client's Library; only its place on the board goes.

operations.summary: Pin things the client said onto the story board, as sticky notes.
operations.description: One or more notes, each the client's own words: reworded at most so it reads as a note (person, tense, unneeded words), never with a claim, fact or adjective added. Each needs the sentence it came from (`quote`), one emoji saying what it is about (e.g. 💇 the work, 👪 people, 💬 something a customer said, 📍 the place) and a theme; naming a theme the board does not have yet starts it. Afterwards tell the client in one line, e.g. "I've put four of your sayings on the story board — heart the ones that are most you, and thumbs-down anything that's off."

notes.description: The notes, each `{"text": ..., "quote": ..., "emoji": ..., "theme": ...}` — `quote` the client's original sentence, `theme` a theme's name or id.

operations.summary: Reword a note on the story board, or change its emoji.
operations.description: For a note the client gave 👎, or one that reads badly. Never a note the client wrote, edited, hearted or gave 👍: that wording is theirs and the change is refused. A reworded 👎 note loses its 👎, because the client has not seen the new words yet. Changing only the emoji is allowed on any note.

text.description: The new wording, still the client's words.

emoji.description: One emoji saying what the note is about.

operations.summary: Move a note on the story board to another theme.
operations.description: When the client asks for it, or when a note sits better under another theme. Naming a theme the board does not have yet starts it.

operations.summary: Take one of your notes off the story board.
operations.description: Only a note you pinned that the client has not made theirs; a note they wrote, edited, hearted or gave 👍 stays until they delete it.

operations.summary: Add a theme to the story board, or rename one.
operations.description: A theme groups notes about one thing — the work, the family, the place. Its name is written on the board and its notes take its colour. At most six themes. Give `theme` to rename that one; leave it out to add a new one.

theme.description: The id or current name of the theme to rename.

operations.summary: Offer the client two or three headlines at the top of the story board.
operations.description: One line each that a stranger reads on the home page, answering why the right customer would pick them over what they would otherwise choose — not a strategy statement. Write them from the notes the client hearted and name those notes in `from`; a headline from nothing is refused. Recommend one with `pick`. The client steps through them, chooses one, or writes their own. Offered lines they did not choose are never offered again. After they have chosen, a new offer waits beside their choice as new options and never replaces it. One round costs one exchange: if nothing lands, move on and settle the headline in the draft.

options.description: Two or three headlines, one line each.

pick.description: The index (from 0) of the one you recommend.

from.description: The ids of the hearted notes the headlines are written from.

groups.title: Reading the plan
groups.description: The site's plan as it stands. Nothing here changes anything.

groups.title: Keeping the brief
groups.description: What the client has said about their business, goals and features, and notes beside them.

groups.title: Planning the work
groups.description: The consultant's part: proposing decisions, owning the tasks, answering checks, and putting a look the client chose onto their page.

groups.title: Coordinating the plan
groups.description: The coordinator's part: recording the client's answers to decisions and tracking task progress. Nothing here is an opinion of the site.

groups.title: Keeping the client's questions
groups.description: The questions waiting for the client on their panel: adding and rewording them, withdrawing ones that no longer apply, filling them in from what the client uploaded, and recording the client's yes to a contact detail appearing on the site.

groups.title: Keeping the milestones
groups.description: The checks raised at the milestones of a build, and the stages the build is in: recording that a check was asked and what the client answered, and marking each stage as the work on it starts and finishes.

groups.title: Keeping the comp board
groups.description: The comparable sites you and the client look at before the first build, and what the client likes and dislikes about each.

groups.title: Keeping the story board
groups.description: The client's story in their own words: pinning, rewording, moving and removing notes, naming the themes they cluster under, and offering headlines written from the notes the client hearted.
